knowledge-base.overview: Language-specific idioms, guardrails, and patterns for Java 17+. Loaded automatically when agents work on .java, pom.xml, or build.gradle files. Covers modern Java patterns (records, sealed classes, pattern matching), streams, Optional, resource management, testing with JUnit 5 and AssertJ, and Maven/Gradle tooling for enterprise and Spring Boot applications.

core-principles.principle: Prefer records, `final` fields, and unmodifiable collections. Mutable state is opt-in.
Clear type declarations, no raw types, no unchecked casts. Wildcard imports are forbidden.
Validate inputs at boundaries using `Objects.requireNonNull` and guard checks. Never allow invalid state to propagate.
Favor delegation and interfaces over deep class hierarchies.

guardrail.rule: Never use Optional.get() without a prior isPresent() check. Use orElseThrow(), orElse(), map(), or flatMap() instead.
guardrail.bad: Optional<User> user = userRepository.findById(id); String name = user.get().getName(); // throws NoSuchElementException silently

guardrail.rule: Always use try-with-resources for AutoCloseable types (connections, streams, readers). Never rely on finalize().
Never use raw types. Always parameterize generics. Raw types lose type safety at compile time.
guardrail.bad: List items = new ArrayList(); // raw type, unsafe Map map = new HashMap();
guardrail.good: List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>(); Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();

guardrail.rule: Never use wildcard imports (`import java.util.*`). All imports must be explicit.
Never use Optional as a method parameter or field type. Use it only as a return type for methods that may produce no value.
guardrail.bad: public void process(Optional<User> user) { ... } // confusing contract private Optional<String> name; // field — use nullable instead
guardrail.good: public Optional<User> findById(String id) { ... } // return type only

guardrail.rule: Prefer records for immutable data carriers over hand-written POJOs. Add compact constructors for validation.
Avoid parallel streams unless measured to be faster. Parallel stream overhead is real and can degrade performance for small collections or I/O-bound work.
guardrail.bad: List<String> names = users.parallelStream() .map(User::name) .toList(); // overhead dominates for small lists

guardrail.rule: Do not use streams for side effects. Streams are for transformations. Use enhanced for-loops or forEach separately for mutations.
guardrail.good: List<User> active = users.stream() .filter(User::isActive) .toList(); active.forEach(u -> u.setProcessed(true)); // mutation outside pipeline

guardrail.rule: Pin dependency versions explicitly. Never use dynamic versions such as `1.+` in Maven or Gradle.
Use `var` only when the type is unambiguous from the right-hand side of the assignment. Never use it to obscure types at API boundaries.
guardrail.bad: var result = service.process(input); // type of 'result' unclear without reading service
guardrail.good: var connection = dataSource.getConnection(); // type obvious var statement = connection.prepareStatement(sql); // type obvious

guardrail.rule: Use sealed classes/interfaces for restricted type hierarchies. Enables exhaustive switch pattern matching and makes closed domains explicit.
Prefer `toList()` (Java 16+) over `collect(Collectors.toList())`. The new form is concise and returns an unmodifiable list.

directory.purpose: REST controllers — HTTP concerns only, no business logic
Data access — JPA repositories, JDBC templates

project-structure.note: Packages map to bounded contexts, not technical layers at the top level. Test structure mirrors source structure exactly.

pattern.name: Records for Immutable Data
pattern.context: Any immutable data carrier (DTO, value object, domain event)
pattern.description: Records replace hand-written POJOs: equals, hashCode, toString, and accessors are auto-generated. Use compact constructors for validation.

pattern.name: Sealed Classes with Pattern Matching
pattern.context: Closed domain modelling — result types, state machines, discriminated unions
pattern.description: Sealed classes + switch expressions give exhaustive pattern matching without default fallthrough.

pattern.name: Immutable Collections
pattern.description: Use factory methods for immutable collections. Defensive copy mutable inputs with List.copyOf.

pattern.name: Text Blocks for SQL and JSON
pattern.context: Multi-line string literals — SQL queries, JSON templates
pattern.description: Text blocks preserve indentation and eliminate manual escaping. Always use parameterized queries — never interpolate values.
pattern.example: String query = """ SELECT u.id, u.email, u.created_at FROM users u WHERE u.active = true AND u.role = ? ORDER BY u.created_at DESC LIMIT ? """;

pattern.name: Optional Chaining
pattern.context: Nullable return values — repository lookups, config reads
pattern.description: Chain Optional operations without calling get(). Use ifPresentOrElse for logging branches.

pattern.name: Streams for Transformation
pattern.description: Streams express intent clearly. Keep the pipeline pure; avoid side effects inside stream operations.

testing.framework: JUnit 5 with AssertJ assertions and Mockito mocking

rules.rule: Use @DisplayName for complex scenarios, @Nested to group related tests
Prefer AssertJ over JUnit assertions for readability

Use for closed type hierarchies; enables exhaustive switch pattern matching
Return type only — never parameter or field; never call .get()
Transformations only — no side effects inside pipeline; use toList() not Collectors.toList()
Only after profiling; overhead is real for small collections or I/O
Mandatory for all AutoCloseable (connections, streams, channels)
Forbidden — all imports must be explicit
Only when type is obvious from right side; not at API boundaries
Use for multi-line SQL and JSON; always parameterize values
List.of(), Map.of(), Set.of(), List.copyOf() for defensive copies
Always pin explicitly; run OWASP check before adding new deps
JUnit 5 + AssertJ + Mockito; @ParameterizedTest for data-driven cases
